An inner product on $V = \mathbb{R}^3$ is given by $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle =  3 x_1 y_1 + x_2 y_2 + 7 x_3 y_3.$ Find $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle,$ if

e-5542.worked_solution:
Computing the inner product according to the definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y⟩ & =3{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+7{x}_{3}{y}_{3} \\  & =3\cdot 1\cdot (-3)+(-2)\cdot 1+7\cdot 0\cdot 5 \\  & =-9-2+0 \\  & =-11.\end{aligned}

e-5543.knowledge_point: Calculating the Inner Product of Two Vectors in a Vector Space of Polynomials
e-5543.problem:
Let $V=\mathbb{R}_2[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $2$, equipped with the inner product 

$$
\langle {x}(t), {y}(t) \rangle = x(1)y(1) + x(2)y(2) + x(3)y(3).
$$

 Find $\langle \mathbf{x}(t), \mathbf{y}(t) \rangle,$ if

$$
{x}(t) = 1-2t+3t^2,
	\quad
	{y}(t) = t-t^2.
$$
e-5543.worked_solution:
Computing the inner product according to the definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩ & =x(1)y(1)+x(2)y(2)+x(3)y(3) \\  & =2\cdot 0+9\cdot (-2)+22\cdot (-6) \\  & =0-18-132 \\  & =-150.\end{aligned}
$$

e-5544.knowledge_point: Calculating the Inner Product of Two Vectors in a Vector Space of Continuous Functions
e-5544.problem:
Let $V=\mathcal{C}\left[0,2\pi\right],$ the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $\left[0,2\pi\right].$ Find $\langle \sin t, \cos t \rangle$ if the inner product on $V$ is defined as

$$
\langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi} x(t) y(t) \, \textrm{d}t.
$$
e-5544.worked_solution:
We need to evaluate

$$
\langle \sin t, \cos t \rangle  =  \int_{0}^{2\pi}\sin{t} \cos{t} \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\sin2t =2\sin t\cos t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}(1-1) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is given by $⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+5{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ Find $⟨x,y⟩$, if

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Computing the inner product according to the definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y⟩ & ={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+5{x}_{3}{y}_{3} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 2+(-2)\cdot (0)+5\cdot 0\cdot 1 \\  & =-2+0+0 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Let $V=C[0,2],$ the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,2].$ Find $⟨t,{e}^{t}⟩$ if the inner product on $V$ is defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We need to evaluate

$$
⟨t,{e}^{t}⟩={\int }_{0}^{2}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{t} & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting into the formula for the integration by parts, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{0}^{2}-{\int }_{0}^{2}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t{e}^{t}){|}_{0}^{2}-{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(2{e}^{2}-0{e}^{0})-{e}^{t}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2{e}^{2}-({e}^{2}-1) \\  & ={e}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$
